anchor: Alas! nor dew nor smiling rose
title: The poem: Nâbî's muhammes on what is 'mine'
short: A devotional muhammes (five-line stanzas) by Nâbî (1642-1712), the master of the reflective 'hikemî' style: the poet confesses that nothing in the world is truly his.
body: Nâbî (Yusuf, born at Ruha, now Şanlıurfa, in 1642, died in Istanbul in 1712) is the leading representative of the 'hikemî' (wisdom, didactic) style in Ottoman poetry, which put thought before ornament; his Hayriyye, a book of advice to his son, was widely read. Gibb's heading gives the opening line in transliteration as 'Bu gülistânda benim içün ne gül ne şebnem var' ('in this rose-garden there is for me neither rose nor dew'). The poem has thirteen stanzas, each of four rhyming lines and a fixed refrain. The theme is the Sufi doctrine that all being belongs to God and that the self owns nothing, not even its existence.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, Ottoman Poems Translated into English Verse in the Original Forms (London: Trübner, 1882), Nâbî, Mukhammes, pp. 113-115, and notes 228-229, p. 259

anchor: O that I knew what here I am
title: The refrain
short: Every stanza ends with the same question: what am I here, and what is truly mine? The answer the stanzas give is: nothing.
body: In a muhammes the fifth line of each stanza may be a fixed refrain, as here. The refrain is a question rather than a statement, and the four lines before it change their approach: first a list of things the poet lacks (st. 1), then a list of what God gives (st. 2), then the world as God's handiwork (st. 4), then the self as borrowed and dependent (sts. 5-8), then the poet's powerlessness (st. 10), then the metaphysics of creation (sts. 11-13). The steady return of the question gives the poem its humility, a characteristic note of Nâbî's reflective poetry.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, Ottoman Poems Translated into English Verse in the Original Forms (London: Trübner, 1882), pp. 113-115

title: The world as garden and bazaar
short: The world is a rose-garden where the poet has neither rose nor dew, and a market where he has neither goods nor coin.
body: Two of the commonest figures for the world are joined: the garden (gülistan, 'mead'), whose roses fade, and the bazaar, where everyone trades for gain. The poet has no share in either; 'nor more nor less' means he has neither surplus nor lack of his own. The theme of the stanza is poverty (fakr) in the Sufi sense: to possess nothing and to know it is the beginning of wisdom. The third stanza returns to the 'mart'.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, Ottoman Poems Translated into English Verse in the Original Forms (London: Trübner, 1882), p. 113
Annemarie Schimmel, Mystical Dimensions of Islam (Chapel Hill: University of North Carolina Press, 1975)

anchor: Being 's the bounty of the Lord
title: Being as God's gift
greek: Arabic wujūd ('existence'); Turkish vücûd; waḥdat al-wujūd ('unity of being')
short: Existence, life, breath, speech, body and soul are all God's gifts, not the poet's possessions.
body: The second stanza lists the parts of the human person and assigns each to God. Behind it lies the Sufi doctrine of the unity of being (vahdet-i vücûd), associated with Ibn Arabi, according to which only God truly exists and creatures have a borrowed existence. Nâbî does not argue the doctrine but draws its moral: claims of ownership and of power are pretension. 'The Body is the pile of God' uses 'pile' in its old sense of a large building or edifice (OED, s.v. 'pile', n.).

sources.cite: TDV contributor, 'Vahdet-i Vücûd', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi
E. J. W. Gibb, Ottoman Poems Translated into English Verse in the Original Forms (London: Trübner, 1882), p. 113

title: The breath of God
greek: Arabic nafakhtu fīhi min rūḥī ('I breathed into him of My spirit')
short: The soul is God's breath: an allusion to the Qur'anic account of Adam, into whom God breathed of His spirit.
body: The Qur'an says of the creation of Adam that God fashioned him and 'breathed into him of My spirit' (15:29; 38:72). Sufi writers made this breath the link between the human soul and God. Stanza 7 returns to it: 'My breath is from the Breath of God's benignant Mercy fed', where the 'Breath of the Merciful' (nefes-i Rahmân) was a technical term in Ibn Arabi's school for the creative outpouring of being.

sources.cite: Annemarie Schimmel, Mystical Dimensions of Islam (Chapel Hill: University of North Carolina Press, 1975)

title: Saying 'I'
short: The poet has no right to say 'I am!': selfhood (benlik) is the great illusion that the Sufi path tries to dissolve.
body: Saying 'I' was, for Sufi moralists, the root of pride: Iblis refused to bow to Adam with the words 'I am better than he' (Qur'an 7:12). The famous cry of al-Hallaj, 'I am the Truth', stands at the opposite pole, where the self is annihilated in God. Nâbî's poem is not ecstatic; it takes the sober line that a servant has 'no power of heart' to claim existence at all. The theme returns in stanza 6: 'Nonentity 's my attribute: to Be is of the Lord'.

sources.cite: Annemarie Schimmel, Mystical Dimensions of Islam (Chapel Hill: University of North Carolina Press, 1975)

title: Life held in trust
short: Existence is a loan and life a deposit held in trust; the Qur'an speaks of the 'trust' that heaven and earth refused and humanity accepted.
body: Emanet is something entrusted to a person for safe keeping and to be returned. The Qur'an (33:72) says that God offered 'the trust' to the heavens, the earth and the mountains, and they refused it, but man bore it. Sufi and moral writers read the trust as life, reason, the soul or religious responsibility. Stanza 2 already calls the powers of the body 'His Glory's trust'. Nâbî's point is ethical: what is held in trust cannot be claimed as property, so 'a claim to Power' is arrogance.

title: 'My servant'
short: The highest honour the poet can hope for is that God should call him 'My servant'.
body: In Islamic piety servanthood ('ubûdiyyet) is the summit of human dignity, not a humiliation. The Qur'an calls the Prophet 'His servant' at the most exalted moment of his life, the Night Journey (17:1), and God addresses believers as 'My servants' (39:53). Gibb's 'slave' renders kul, the usual Turkish word for God's servant (and also for the sultan's servants). The stanza moves from the arrogance of claiming power to the grace of being claimed.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, Ottoman Poems Translated into English Verse in the Original Forms (London: Trübner, 1882), p. 114

title: Being and non-being; the Seen and the Unseen
greek: Arabic ʿadam ('non-being'), ʿālam al-shahāda / ʿālam al-ghayb ('world of the seen / unseen')
short: The poet's own attribute is non-being; existence and the 'sea' of the seen and unseen worlds belong to God.
body: Theology distinguished the visible world (âlem-i şehâdet) from the unseen world (âlem-i gayb); the Qur'an calls God 'Knower of the unseen and the seen' (59:22). The 'sea' of both whose waves surge is God's creative activity. The pair 'Being or Non-being' (vücûd and adem) is the language of the unity-of-being school, in which created things are in themselves non-existent and receive existence from God at every moment.

sources.cite: TDV contributor, 'Vahdet-i Vücûd', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi

title: Daily bread and allotted portion
short: Bread, breath, portion and provision all come from God's table; nothing can be taken that has not been allotted.
body: Stanzas 7 and 8 develop the doctrine of rızk, divinely allotted provision: the Qur'an says that there is no creature on earth whose provision is not upon God (11:6). Nâbî sets it out in homely terms, a bounteous table and a kitchen, and then as a principle: 'I cannot, unallotted, take my share from wet or dry'. The 'wet or dry', 'land or ocean', 'silver or gold' pairs (merisms) sweep in everything. Nâbî's reflective verse is often proverbial in this way, and many of his lines circulated as sayings.

title: The Pen and the picture-book of creation
greek: Arabic qalam ('pen'); Persian Shāhnāma ('Book of Kings')
short: Events are lines drawn by the Pen of creation, and human beings are the pictures in creation's great illustrated 'Book of Kings'.
body: The Qur'an swears 'by the Pen' (68:1) and speaks of God 'who taught by the pen' (96:4); in tradition the first thing God created was the Pen, which wrote all that would be on the Preserved Tablet. Nâbî makes the world a manuscript: illuminated scroll, woven garment and, finally, a Shâhnâma, Firdawsī's Persian epic, of which manuscripts were richly illustrated. Gibb's note explains that copies of the Shâhnâma were usually decorated with miniatures showing the course of the story, so men are figures in a picture painted by another hand.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, Ottoman Poems Translated into English Verse in the Original Forms (London: Trübner, 1882), note 228, p. 259

anchor: Whilst in the womb I lay
title: Created in the womb
short: God brought the poet out of nothingness and provided for all his needs even in the womb, with kindnesses hidden and visible.
body: The Qur'an describes human creation 'in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation, in three darknesses' (39:6), and the stages of the embryo (23:12-14). Nâbî's stanza follows the life from nothingness ('adem) to birth and upbringing. The last line, 'With me He drew a curtain o'er Distinction's beauty dear', is obscure in Gibb's English; it seems to say that God veiled from the poet the beauty of the divine order or of his own rank, but the sense is uncertain and should be checked against the Turkish.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, Ottoman Poems Translated into English Verse in the Original Forms (London: Trübner, 1882), p. 115

title: The Hidden Treasure
greek: Arabic kanz makhfī ('hidden treasure'); Turkish kenz-i mahfî
short: The surging sea of the world is the showing-forth of the Hidden Treasure: God, who wished to be known and so created the world.
body: A saying attributed to God, much loved by the Sufis, runs: 'I was a hidden treasure; I wished to be known, so I created creation in order to be known.' Ibn Arabi and his followers took the 'hidden treasure' to be the divine essence, and the created world as its self-disclosure. Hadith scholars doubted its authenticity, but in mystical poetry it is everywhere. For Nâbî the 'raging main' of changing appearances is that disclosure, 'this Majesty made plain'.

sources.cite: TDV contributor, 'Kenz-i Mahfî', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi
Annemarie Schimmel, Mystical Dimensions of Islam (Chapel Hill: University of North Carolina Press, 1975)

title: The world as a mirror; the store-houses of possibility
short: The storehouses of possible things fill and empty; the world is a glass-lined mirror in which the two lights, sun and moon, cast their phases.
body: 'Possibility's store-houses' renders a philosophical term: the mümkinât are contingent beings, things that may or may not exist, as opposed to God, the Necessary Being. They come into being and pass away, 'now void, now full'. Gibb's note: the 'Lights Twain' are the Sun and Moon, and the world is a mirror in which the influences of the planets are reflected. In Sufi metaphysics the world is also the mirror of the divine names.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, Ottoman Poems Translated into English Verse in the Original Forms (London: Trübner, 1882), note 229, p. 259
TDV contributor, 'Vahdet-i Vücûd', TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi

title: The old vineyard in autumn
short: The last image: the world is an old vineyard ruined by autumn's blast, returning to the garden of the opening stanza.
body: The poem began in a rose-garden where the poet had neither rose nor dew; it ends in a vineyard ruined by autumn. The garden and its seasons are the traditional figure for the transience of the world (spring for youth and prosperity, autumn for decay and death). The preceding line, 'The blinded thing — in scattering strange fruits its hours are past', is hard; it may refer to the world (or time) as a blind sower. The final refrain then asks its question once more, now against the ruin of everything that seemed to belong to us.

sources.cite: E. J. W. Gibb, Ottoman Poems Translated into English Verse in the Original Forms (London: Trübner, 1882), p. 115
